pharm: A long-acting, selective peripheral histamine H1-receptor antagonist with additional mast-cell-stabilizing and anti-inflammatory activity, used for allergic rhinitis and urticaria; it has a weak potential to prolong the QT interval.
quick: One 10 mg modified-release tablet once daily
May be taken with or without food; swallow whole, do not chew
Avoid, especially first trimester; safety not established
Not recommended; excreted in breast milk
Little effect on clearance; half-life modestly prolonged in chronic renal insufficiency
Contraindicated in significantly impaired hepatic function
Symptom control; cardiac/QT risk factors and interacting drugs
summary: Mizolastine is a second-generation, long-acting H1-antihistamine approved in the EU/UK (e.g., Mizollen) for the symptomatic relief of seasonal and perennial allergic rhinoconjunctivitis and of urticaria; it is not FDA-approved (data below are based on the EMA/SmPC and BNF). It is taken as a single 10 mg modified-release tablet once daily, is largely non-sedating, and also has mast-cell-stabilizing and anti-inflammatory properties. Because it can weakly prolong the QT interval and is metabolized via hepatic glucuronidation/sulphation (with CYP3A4-sensitive clearance), it is contraindicated in significant cardiac disease or QT prolongation, in significant hepatic impairment, and with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors such as macrolide antibiotics and systemic imidazole/azole antifungals. Onset of action is rapid (about 1 hour) and effect persists for about 24 hours.
indications: Symptomatic relief of seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis (hay fever)
Symptomatic relief of perennial allergic rhinoconjunctivitis

dosage.n: One modified-release tablet; swallow whole with water
Avoid in clinically significant cardiac disease, arrhythmia history, or QT prolongation

admin: Swallow the modified-release tablet whole with water - do not chew, crush, or divide
Take one 10 mg tablet once daily, at about the same time each day
May be taken with or without food
Do not exceed the recommended dose (higher doses increase QT-prolongation risk)
Review concomitant medicines for CYP3A4 inhibitors and other QT-prolonging drugs before starting
moa: Mizolastine is a potent, selective antagonist of peripheral histamine H1-receptors. By blocking H1 receptors on vascular endothelium, smooth muscle, and other effector cells it inhibits the histamine-mediated effects of allergic responses - vasodilation, increased vascular permability, pruritus, and mucosal secretion - relieving the symptoms of allergic rhinitis and urticaria. In addition to H1 blockade it stabilizes mast cells (reducing histamine release) and has anti-inflammatory actions, including inhibition of mediator release and effects on inflammatory cell influx. Its limited penetration of the central nervous system accounts for its largely non-sedating profile.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to mizolastine or any excipient
Clinically significant cardiac disease or history of symptomatic arrhythmias
Clinically significant bradycardia or electrolyte imbalance (e.g., hypokalemia)
Concomitant macrolide antibiotics or systemic imidazole/azole antifungals
Concomitant Class I or Class III antiarrhythmics or other QT-prolonging drugs
relative: Elderly patients (greater susceptibility to cardiac effects)
monitor: Cardiac risk factors and QT-prolonging comedication
Serum electrolytes where arrhythmia risk exists

preg: Use should be avoided during pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester, because safety has not been established; there are insufficient human data. Use only if clearly necessary and after assessing benefit versus risk.
lact: Mizolastine is excreted in breast milk and is not recommended during breastfeeding. If treatment is required, a decision should be made to either stop nursing or avoid the drug.
renal: Bodyweight and creatinine clearance have little influence on the oral clearance of mizolastine. In chronic renal insufficiency the terminal elimination half-life was prolonged by about 47% compared with healthy young volunteers; routine dose adjustment is generally not required, but use caution in severe impairment.
hepatic: Contraindicated in significantly impaired hepatic function. Mizolastine is extensively metabolized in the liver (glucuronidation and sulphation), and impaired hepatic function plus reduced metabolic clearance can increase exposure and the risk of QT prolongation.

major: Macrolide antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin, clarithromycin) - CYP3A4 inhibition raises mizolastine levels and QT risk; contraindicated
Systemic imidazole/azole antifungals (e.g., ketoconazole) - increase exposure and QT risk; contraindicated
Class I and Class III antiarrhythmics and other QT-prolonging drugs - additive QT prolongation; contraindicated
moderate: Other potent CYP3A4 inhibitors - may increase plasma concentrations
Other QT-prolonging agents (e.g., certain antipsychotics, antiemetics, fluoroquinolones) - additive cardiac risk
CNS depressants / alcohol - possible additive sedation in susceptible patients
minor: No clinically significant interaction reported with lorazepam in pharmacodynamic studies
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food does not require dose adjustment.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid or limit alcohol; additive central depressant effects are possible in some individuals.
interactions.diagnostics: May suppress skin-prick allergy test responses; discontinue antihistamines for an appropriate interval before skin testing. Monitor ECG/QT where indicated.

serious: Significant hepatic enzyme elevation / hepatic dysfunction
rare: Cardiac arrhythmia (in predisposed patients or overdose)
emergency: Syncope or arrhythmia from QT prolongation

monitoring: Cardiac risk factors, QT-prolonging comedication, and electrolytes where arrhythmia risk exists
ECG if used in patients with cardiac risk (although high-risk patients are contraindicated)
Hepatic status if symptoms suggest hepatic effects
counsel: Take one 10 mg tablet once a day and swallow it whole with water - do not chew or crush it
Do not take more than one tablet a day; taking extra can affect your heart rhythm
Tell your doctor about all your other medicines - some antibiotics, antifungals, and heart-rhythm drugs must not be combined with this
Although usually non-drowsy, it can make some people sleepy - see how it affects you before driving
Avoid or limit alcohol while taking it
Stop antihistamines for the time your allergist advises before any skin allergy testing
Get medical help if you have fainting, palpitations, or swelling of the face/lips/throat
pk: Plasma Tmax about 1 hour; oral bioavailability ~65%
Effect persists up to about 24 hours - supports once-daily dosing
Store in a cool, dry place, protected from light and out of reach of children
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - data are based on the EMA/SmPC and BNF (EU/UK; e.g., Mizollen)
One 10 mg modified-release tablet once daily; swallow whole
Largely non-sedating with mast-cell-stabilizing and anti-inflammatory activity
Weak QT-prolongation potential - contraindicated in significant cardiac disease, QT prolongation, and significant hepatic impairment
Avoid with macrolides, systemic azole antifungals, and other QT-prolonging or potent CYP3A4-inhibiting drugs
Increased appetite and weight gain are recognized adverse effects
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for the next day's dose, skip the missed one and continue with your regular once-daily schedule. Do not take two tablets at the same time or take an extra tablet to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Overdose may cause drowsiness and, importantly, an increased risk of QT-interval prolongation and cardiac arrhythmia. There is no specific antidote. Manage with gastric emptying/activated charcoal if recent and appropriate, continuous ECG and cardiac monitoring (correcting electrolytes), and symptomatic and supportive care; treatment cannot be removed effectively by dialysis (high protein binding).
